text: Candlelight flickers across the customs officer's desk as he leans over the manifest, eyes narrowing. Forty barrels of salt. A palpable tension fills the room. Shockingly, the duty on those barrels would swallow every penny of the merchant's profit.
strengths: contains a real stake, the duty against the profit
weaknesses: describes light and gestures the picture already shows
tells the listener the room is tense
a hype adverb announces surprise instead of earning it
spokenRhythm: Atmospheric description, a dropped fragment, a stock mood line, then the one fact arriving too late.
narrativeFunction: Meant to raise the stakes of a customs inspection, but spends most of its words on what the camera can do.
whyItFails: Three of four sentences duplicate the picture or instruct the audience how to feel. The only information, that the duty would take the whole profit, is buried at the end behind an adverb that sounds like a generic history video.
rewrite: The manifest on the customs officer's desk listed forty barrels of salt. The duty on them would take every penny of the merchant's profit.

text: Picture this. Deep beneath the earth, a boy of ten crouches in the darkness, a single candle flickering beside him. Can you feel the damp? Can you hear the timbers creak? For twelve hours a day, he opened and closed a wooden trapdoor so that air could reach the men at the coal face.
strengths: the trapdoor and the twelve-hour day are strong, specific facts
weaknesses: orders the listener to imagine what the screen is already showing
two rhetorical questions in a row about sensations
slides from present to past tense when the facts finally arrive
spokenRhythm: A two-word command, a long descriptive sentence, two short questions, then the facts in one long final line.
narrativeFunction: Meant to put the audience underground with a child at work, but spends its words doing the picture's job.
whyItFails: The opener and the questions are the reflexes of machine-written history narration. The darkness and the candle belong to the camera, and the feelings the questions ask for are ones the facts would produce without help. What the boy did, and for how long, is held back until the last line.
rewrite: Underground, a boy of ten opened and closed a wooden trapdoor so that air could reach the men at the coal face. He did it for twelve hours a day.

text: The hut. The stove. The fuel. One tin left, and forty days until the relief ship. The plan? Ration everything. But fate had other plans.
strengths: two hard facts, the single tin and the forty days, sit inside it
weaknesses: three fragments in a row as a fake drumroll
a question answered at once by a fragment
ends on a stock tease instead of the next fact
spokenRhythm: Staccato nouns, one real sentence, a question and answer, then a portentous closing line.
narrativeFunction: Meant to establish the predicament in the hut, but performs suspense instead of explaining it.
whyItFails: The fragments list objects the picture can show. The question and answer pair is filler. The closing line promises disaster without delivering any information, which is the shape of a trailer, not a documentary.
rewrite: In the hut, there was one tin of fuel left for the stove. The relief ship was forty days away, and the plan was to ration everything.

text: The assay office — a cramped wooden shack at the end of a muddy street — was the beating heart of the town, a pressure cooker where dreams lived and died on the turn of a scale. The stage was set. Every nugget that crossed its counter was a roll of the dice with destiny — and the assayer's word decided what it was worth.
strengths: the assayer's power over value is a real and interesting point
weaknesses: four figures of speech piled on one building
em-dashes do the work of sentences
destiny and the stage was set are trailer clichés
spokenRhythm: One overloaded sentence broken by dashes, a stock four-word line, then another dash-split sentence.
narrativeFunction: Meant to show why the assay office mattered, but buries the reason under metaphors.
whyItFails: A listener cannot hold a heart, a pressure cooker, dreams and dice in one breath. The em-dashes are page syntax that a voice cannot perform. The single useful idea, that one man's word set the value of everything found, is the last clause of the last sentence.
rewrite: The assay office was a small wooden building at the end of the street. For every nugget that crossed its counter, the assayer's word decided what it was worth.

text: In the dim back room of the print shop, the compositor's fingers fly across the type case. He pauses and glances at the door. Here's the thing. The sheet he was setting had no licence, and little did he know, the town's searchers were already on their way.
strengths: the unlicensed sheet and the searchers give real stakes
weaknesses: invents gestures for a reconstruction and narrates them
a truth-reveal phrase stands in for a transition
the stock phrase claims to know what he did not know
spokenRhythm: Two descriptive sentences, a three-word throat-clearing line, then a long sentence carrying all the information.
narrativeFunction: Meant to build tension in the print shop, but uses gestures and a cliché where the rule and the risk would do.
whyItFails: Flying fingers and a glance at the door are the picture's business, and here they are invented. Here's the thing and little did he know are phrases listeners now hear as machine narration. The real tension, an illegal job and the searchers coming, needs no help.
rewrite: In the back room of the print shop, the compositor was setting a sheet that had no licence. The town's searchers were already on their way.
